<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
I have a solid picture. The user wants an evaluation and plan for the most suitable format for longitudinal mouse recording.

Reviewing continuous video recorder timing sidecar patterns to finalize the recommendation.

SQLite with WAL mode is the leading candidate. It provides crash tolerance, native microsecond datetime precision, and efficient append operations. CSV export is straightforward. The event-driven design prevents idle bloat.

SQLite offers time-range queries without loading the entire dataset. It is a single portable file with no external dependencies. Memory stays low because inserts can stream without buffering all samples. Parquet is poor for live capture because appending requires rewriting row groups. It is better suited for post-capture analysis.

DuckDB and HDF5 are too heavy and lack proper crash safety for this producer app. NDJSON and CSV streaming are viable but lack random access and proper database semantics. Parquet could serve as a secondary export format.

Arrow IPC and Feather share Parquet's live append limitations. Reconstructing absolute time from filenames is fragile. The recommended schema uses an integer microsecond UTC epoch for wall time, nullable x and y coordinates, a monotonic relative timestamp, and a session identifier. Event-driven inserts will record movement and compacted idle heartbeats. A bounded in-memory ring will hold preview data while full history persists on disk. A dedicated export path will regenerate compatible CSV files with relative millisecond timestamps from session start.

CSV streaming can remain as a secondary export path or be replaced by SQLite as the primary store. The capture loop should continue using OS hooks rather than fixed polling, writing only when the mouse position actually changes. True microsecond wall-clock precision is platform-dependent; `time.time_ns()` is required on Windows, and monotonic timestamps should use `perf_counter_ns()`.

Storing both wall-clock and high-resolution monotonic timestamps aligns with LSL and EEG standards. The response should be an architecture evaluation plan rather than immediate implementation.

The deliverable will combine an architecture evaluation with a concrete implementation outline for IOGraph. CSV streaming will be preserved as an optional export path rather than replaced by SQLite.
</details></think>

{
  "name": "SQLite mouse DB",
  "overview": "Recommend SQLite (WAL) as the canonical longitudinal mouse store: microsecond wall-clock timestamps, event-driven idle-compact appends, bounded RAM, and CSV export that preserves the existing x,y,time relative-ms contract for PhoPyMNEHelper/pyPhoTimeline.",
  "plan": "# Longitudinal mouse store: SQLite WAL + CSV export\n\n## Verdict\n\n**Use SQLite in WAL mode as the primary durable format.** It is the best fit for crash-tolerant, multi-day quantified-self / neuroscience mouse logging with easy CSV export and low idle cost. Keep the existing `x,y,time` CSV as an **export / optional stream** format only—not the system of record.\n\nFormat comparison (summary):\n\n- **SQLite + WAL**: best crash durability, live append, µs datetime, idle-friendly inserts, indexed longitudinal queries, trivial CSV export, stdlib-only packaging\n- **Continuous CSV (current)**: partial crash safety (~1 s fsync; queue can drop); relative ms only; weak longitudinal story via many files + filename clocks\n- **NDJSON quit chunks**: weak mid-session durability\n- **Parquet / Arrow / HDF5 / DuckDB**: excellent offline analytics, poor or heavy as a live desktop capture primary; extra deps\n\nParquet/HDF5 remain good **offline analysis** exports later; they are the wrong live writer for a desktop capture loop.\n\n## Why current design is insufficient\n\nCapture today in [`iograph/tracker.py`](c:/Users/pho/repos/EmotivEpoc/ACTIVE_DEV/IOGraph/iograph/tracker.py):\n\n- Polls `QCursor.pos()` at **33 ms**; samples store **relative int ms** from `monotonic()`, not wall-clock µs\n- Holds **all** samples in `_raw_samples` for the whole session (RAM grows with movement)\n- [`CsvStreamWriter`](c:/Users/pho/repos/EmotivEpoc/ACTIVE_DEV/IOGraph/iograph/services/csv_stream.py) already does compact idle + background flush/fsync, but CSV is not a robust longitudinal DB\n- Analysis in [`PhoPyMNEHelper/.../iograph_data.py`](c:/Users/pho/repos/EmotivEpoc/ACTIVE_DEV/PhoPyMNEHelper/src/phopymnehelper/iograph_data.py) expects CSV `x,y,time` with **relative ms** and reconstructs `sample_time` from the filename—so the DB must **not** put wall-clock values in the exported `time` column\n\n## Chosen architecture\n\n```mermaid\nflowchart LR\n  tick[\"TrackCanvas 33ms poll\"] --\u003e gate[\"change or idle-compact\"]\n  gate --\u003e preview[\"bounded preview buffer\"]\n  gate --\u003e q[\"writer queue\"]\n  q --\u003e wal[\"SQLite WAL writer thread\"]\n  wal --\u003e db[\"iograph_mouse.sqlite\"]\n  db --\u003e csvExp[\"CSV export adapter\"]\n  csvExp --\u003e analysis[\"PhoPyMNEHelper / pyPhoTimeline\"]\n```\n\n### File layout\n\n- One rolling DB file (default under the existing CSV output folder or AppData): `iograph_mouse.sqlite`\n- WAL sidecars (`-wal`, `-shm`) while open; clean close checkpoints them\n- Optional later: calendar-month rotation if a single file grows huge (not required for v1)\n\n### Schema (v1)\n\n```sql\nCREATE TABLE sessions (\n  session_id     INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,\n  started_at_us  INTEGER NOT NULL,\n  ended_at_us    INTEGER,\n  app_version    TEXT,\n  host           TEXT\n);\n\nCREATE TABLE samples (\n  session_id  INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES sessions(session_id),\n  t_wall_us   INTEGER NOT NULL,\n  t_mono_us   INTEGER NOT NULL,\n  x           INTEGER,\n  y           INTEGER,\n  PRIMARY KEY (session_id, t_mono_us)\n);\n\nCREATE INDEX idx_samples_wall ON samples(t_wall_us);\n```\n\n- `t_wall_us`: wall UTC microseconds since Unix epoch (canonical absolute time)\n- `t_mono_us`: pause-aware monotonic microseconds for relative export\n- `x`/`y` NULL = idle marker\n\n**Timestamp policy**\n\n- Capture both wall (`time.time_ns() // 1000`) and pause-aware monotonic µs\n- Export CSV `time` as `int(t_mono_us / 1000)` so consumers stay compatible\n- Document platform truth: Windows wall-clock resolution is often ~1 ms even when stored as µs; monotonic/`perf_counter_ns` is better for inter-sample intervals. Optional `lsl_local_clock` can be added later for EEG sync without breaking v1\n\n**Idle policy (no fixed-rate DB growth)**\n\n- Mirror current CSV streamer: while position unchanged, do not insert every tick; keep one pending idle and write/replace only when movement resumes, on pause/stop, or on a ~1 s heartbeat so crash during idle still records last idle time\n- Movement: insert only when `(x,y)` changes (storage is event-driven even though capture remains 33 ms polled)\n\n**Crash tolerance**\n\n- Writer thread: batched `executemany` in short transactions; `PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL`; `synchronous=NORMAL`; commit about every 100–500 ms or N rows\n- Never block the 33 ms UI tick: same non-blocking queue pattern as `CsvStreamWriter` (drop-oldest under extreme backlog)\n- After unclean exit: WAL recovers automatically; start a **new** `sessions` row on next tracking start (simpler integrity than resurrecting an open session)\n\n**Memory / performance**\n\n- Stop treating `_raw_samples` as the longitudinal store for multi-hour/day runs\n- Keep a **bounded** in-memory structure for live preview / Save Image\n- Full history lives only in SQLite; Save Raw Data / CSV export streams from a DB cursor to file\n\n### CSV compatibility bridge\n\nExport must emit:\n\n```text\nx,y,time\n2074,933,55\n,,890\n```\n\nwith absolute-style filename from session `started_at_us` + duration hours (same as [`session_controller.export_base_name`](c:/Users/pho/repos/EmotivEpoc/ACTIVE_DEV/IOGraph/iograph/core/session_controller.py)), so PhoPyMNEHelper start-anchoring keeps working. Optional continuous CSV stream can remain as a secondary sink or be demoted to export-on-stop once SQLite is trusted.\n\nDo not change analysis code in v1.\n\n## Implementation touchpoints (IOGraph only for v1)\n\n- New writer: [`iograph/services/sqlite_stream.py`](c:/Users/pho/repos/EmotivEpoc/ACTIVE_DEV/IOGraph/iograph/services/sqlite_stream.py) — queue, WAL, idle compact, export helpers\n- Capture: [`iograph/tracker.py`](c:/Users/pho/repos/EmotivEpoc/ACTIVE_DEV/IOGraph/iograph/tracker.py) — wall+mono µs; bounded preview\n- Lifecycle/settings: [`iograph/main.py`](c:/Users/pho/repos/EmotivEpoc/ACTIVE_DEV/IOGraph/iograph/main.py) — start/pause/reset/quit; DB path option; footer count\n- Session metadata: [`iograph/core/session_controller.py`](c:/Users/pho/repos/EmotivEpoc/ACTIVE_DEV/IOGraph/iograph/core/session_controller.py) — wall start for export naming\n- Prefer DB over quit-only NDJSON for durability/restore once restore-from-DB exists\n\nReuse the writer-thread design from [`csv_stream.py`](c:/Users/pho/repos/EmotivEpoc/ACTIVE_DEV/IOGraph/iograph/services/csv_stream.py).\n\n## Out of scope\n\n- OS mouse hooks instead of 33 ms polling\n- PhoPyMNEHelper reading SQLite directly\n- Click/button/window-title channels\n- Parquet secondary export\n\n## Validation\n\n- `python3 -m compileall iograph`\n- Unit tests: idle hours to O(1) rows; crash reopen recovers; CSV export matches relative-ms contract\n- Manual: long idle keeps DB size flat; movement inserts at about \u003c=30 Hz; exported CSV loads in PhoPyMNEHelper unchanged\n",

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
I have a clear implementation plan.

Beginning implementation with the SQLite stream writer in `iograph/services/sqlite_stream.py`.

The tracker will compute wall and monotonic timestamps. The sink callback will be extended to pass these alongside the existing sample data. The remaining work covers wiring main.py, adding settings and menu, CSV export, and tests.

The CSV sink's `accept` method only accepts `x`, `y`, `t`, and `appended`, so extra timestamp arguments would cause a failure. A fan-out wrapper in `MainWindow._on_sample` will route samples to both the SQLite writer and the CSV sink separately.

The fan-out wrapper will pass millisecond timestamps to the CSV sink and microsecond timestamps to the SQLite sink. The tracker will supply both wall and monotonic timestamps. A 50,000-sample deque will bound `_raw_samples` for preview.

Bounded `_raw_samples` would truncate the NDJSON restore preview and break clean-quit exports. The v1 approach needs to preserve full history for restore while keeping the preview list small.

Live tracking will write samples to SQLite. The in-memory `_raw_samples` list will be bounded to a small recent window for preview. Save Raw Data will export from SQLite when a session is active. On quit, the app will write NDJSON from the bounded preview or export from SQLite for restore. The simpler v1 restore path will use the current session's database directly.

On quit, the app will persist the SQLite path and session ID in the session state JSON. On load, it will read only the last N samples from the database for preview, or rely on the existing preview cache PNG and restore elapsed time from the database's maximum monotonic timestamp. Loading the full history into memory would defeat the purpose of keeping the preview bounded.

The in-memory `_raw_samples` list will be bounded to 200,000 samples, roughly two hours of continuous movement at 30 Hz. On save, the app will write NDJSON only for this bounded preview window, or skip it entirely when a preview cache is present. On load, elapsed time will be restored from the database's maximum monotonic timestamp, and the last N samples will be loaded into the preview list.

The tracker will store `_run_started_wall_ns` and accumulate monotonic microseconds across pauses. Elapsed time will be computed as accumulated microseconds plus the current monotonic delta, with millisecond values derived from that for backward compatibility. Each sample will record wall-clock time via `time.time_ns() // 1000`. The SQLite writer will use a `SampleRow` tuple containing session ID, wall-clock microseconds, monotonic microseconds, x, and y.

The `SqliteStreamWriter` API is now defined with `start`, `accept`, `flush_pending_idle`, `stop`, and CSV export methods. A one-second idle heartbeat timer in the writer thread will flush pending idle samples. The primary key will be `(session_id, t_mono_us)`, which risks overwriting rows during idle updates.

Pending idle samples will be held in memory and flushed to SQLite only on movement, pause, or heartbeat. This avoids duplicate primary-key rows during idle stretches.

The SQLite idle compaction strategy is refined. A `_last_was_idle` flag will track whether the last row written for a session was idle. If so, the next idle flush will UPDATE that existing row's timestamps while keeping x and y NULL. Otherwise it will INSERT a new row. This avoids duplicate primary-key conflicts during idle stretches. The one-second heartbeat timer will still upsert idle rows to ensure crash-safe persistence.

The idle compaction strategy is refined. Updating the primary-key monotonic timestamp is awkward, so the writer will instead store the open idle rowid and update that row directly. When movement resumes after idle, the rowid is cleared and a new movement row is inserted.

The writer thread will consume a queue of tuples: `("sample", x, y, t_wall, t_mono)`, `("idle", t_wall, t_mono)`, or `("stop",)`. SQLite commits will be batched for efficiency. The database path will be `iograph_mouse.sqlite` in the app directory, and it will persist across sessions so new sessions append to the same file. Resetting during tracking will end the current session and start a new one in that same database. Pausing will flush the pending idle sample and keep the session open, continuing the monotonic timestamp via accumulated time.

Session lifecycle rules are now defined. Pausing flushes idle samples but keeps the session open. Resuming continues the same session without creating a new one. Resetting ends the current session and starts a new one if tracking is still active. Quitting ends the session permanently.

The `_raw_samples` bound is set to 100,000 samples. When the limit is exceeded, the oldest chunk is dropped and the last 80 percent of the list is preserved. The writer will use `ensure_session()`, `flush_pending_idle()`, and `end_session()` methods to manage the session lifecycle.

The raw sample buffer will be pruned only every N appends to avoid per-tick overhead. Elapsed time will be tracked in microseconds using `_accumulated_us` and `_last_elapsed_us`, with `get_elapsed_ms` returning the value in milliseconds. `stop_tracking` must be updated to accumulate microseconds
</details></think>

**On Windows, a second launch is blocked** — including a standalone `.exe`. On macOS/Linux there is no single-instance guard.

```15:45:iograph/app/bootstrap.py
def run_app(window_factory) -> int:
    if sys.platform.startswith("win"):
        QApplication.setHighDpiScaleFactorRoundingPolicy(Qt.HighDpiScaleFactorRoundingPolicy.PassThrough)
    app = QApplication(sys.argv)
    if sys.platform.startswith("win"):
        if not _acquire_windows_single_instance_lock():
            return 0
    window = window_factory()
    window.show()
    return app.exec()

def _acquire_windows_single_instance_lock() -> bool:
    ...
    lock = QLockFile(str(lock_dir / "iograph-single-instance.lock"))
    lock.setStaleLockTime(0)
    if not lock.tryLock(0):
        ...
        QMessageBox.information(..., i18n.tr("app.single_instance.message"), ...)
        return False
```

### Windows (dev and `.exe`)
- Second process takes a `QLockFile` under AppLocalData (`iograph-single-instance.lock`).
- If the lock is held: shows **“IOGraph is already running.”** and exits with code `0` — no second window, no second SQLite/CSV writer.
- Same path for a PyInstaller `.exe`: still goes through `run_app()`, so the guard applies to the frozen build too.
- Stale locks: `setStaleLockTime(0)` means a crashed instance’s lock is **not** auto-cleared by age; you may need to delete the lock file (or reboot/logoff cleanup) if a hard kill left it behind.

### macOS / Linux
- No lock. Multiple instances can run and, if they share the same DB folder, both can open `iograph_mouse.sqlite`.
- SQLite WAL can tolerate concurrent access poorly for two writers: possible `database is locked`, footer “SQLite unavailable”, or two interleaved sessions in one file. Continuous CSV is safer there (unique filename per start).

### Practical takeaway
Accidental double-click of the Windows `.exe` is already handled. The SQLite longitudinal store is **not** designed for multi-writer; the Windows single-instance lock is what keeps that safe. Non-Windows (or a lock failure / stale lock) is the risk path if you care about that.

_**Agent (default)**_

**Short answer:** committed mouse data in SQLite usually survives; the last ~0.25–1s of activity and a clean session/UI restore may not. Windows single-instance lock can also stick after a hard kill.

### Abrupt process crash (Task Manager kill, access violation, power loss mid-write)

| Piece | What survives | What you can lose |
|---|---|---|
| **SQLite samples** | Rows already **committed** (~every 250 ms, or on idle heartbeat/`sync`) | Uncommitted queue batch, plus anything still only in the in-memory pending-idle slot |
| **SQLite session row** | Session exists; `ended_at_us` likely stays `NULL` | Clean end marker / WAL checkpoint on stop |
| **Continuous CSV** | Flushed/fsynced lines (~1 s fsync) | Same order of recent lines; pending idle until next flush |
| **In-memory `_raw_samples` / preview** | Gone | Preview trail in RAM |
| **Quit-time NDJSON + `session_state.json`** | Only written on clean quit | Restore-from-last-session UI state usually missing after hard crash |
| **Single-instance lock (Windows)** | Lock file can remain | Next launch may show “already running” until the OS releases it or the stale lock is removed (`setStaleLockTime(0)` disables age-based stale clearing) |

SQLite WAL is the durable path here: on next open, SQLite replays the `-wal` file and recovers committed transactions. A new tracking start creates a **new** `sessions` row rather than resurrecting the open one.

Idle is a bit special: consecutive idle ticks stay in memory until movement, pause, ~1 s UI heartbeat flush, or stop. A crash during a long idle may lose only the *latest* idle timestamp update, not the movement history.

### User shuts down / restarts the computer

- **Graceful shutdown** (Windows “Shut down” that sends close to apps): IOGraph can run `closeEvent` → flush → save session state → stop writers (including WAL checkpoint). That is close to a normal quit; data and restore metadata should be fine if the OS gives the process time.
- **Forced/fast power-off or kill during shutdown**: same as abrupt crash — last uncommitted ~sub-second of SQLite/CSV can be lost; session JSON/NDJSON may be missing; lock file may be stale until reboot clears process handles (reboot usually fixes the lock; a crash *without* reboot is the stickier case).

### Standalone `.exe`
Same code paths. Packaging does not add extra crash protection or change WAL behavior. The DB still lives in the chosen output folder (not inside the exe).

### Practical expectation
After a hard crash you should still have nearly all movement in `iograph_mouse.sqlite` (minus roughly the last commit window). Reloading the app may not restore the on-screen session the way a clean quit does, and on Windows you might need to clear a stale single-instance lock if relaunch is blocked.
